Snowtrout of the Indus basin exhibit a maximum recorded total length of 63.4 centimeters [Li = 63.4 centimeters], placing them among the larger cyprinids native to high-altitude streams. The species demonstrates a clear sexual dimorphism in size at reproductive maturation, with females achieving the standard length at puberty at 47.9 centimeters [Lp = 47.9 centimeters], a value that likely reflects the additional body cavity volume required for ovarian development and egg retention. Males, in contrast, reach puberty at a notably smaller standard length of 36.9 centimeters [Lp = 36.9 centimeters], a divergence consistent with patterns observed in other Himalayan Schizothorax species where male reproductive investment is heavily skewed toward spawning competition rather than gamete production. These size thresholds were derived from extensive field sampling across altitudinal gradients, where gonadal staging confirmed the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation. The later pubertal attainment in females underscores a life-history strategy prioritizing somatic growth before the heavy metabolic demands of oogenesis, a common adaptation in cold-water teleosts facing short growing seasons.

The fertilised eggs of Schizothorax waltoni are demersal and relatively large for a cyprinid, with an average diameter of 2.5 mm, a trait that enhances yolk reserves for embryonic development in cold, oligotrophic streams. This substantial investment per offspring is reflected in the calculated wet weight at birth of 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams], representing the mass immediately following yolk-sac absorption and the onset of exogenous feeding. Such a value is comparatively high for a teleost of this body size, suggesting a strategy that produces well-provisioned larvae capable of withstanding the brief period between yolk depletion and successful first prey capture. The relationship between egg diameter and hatchling mass follows a cubic function of egg volume, and the computed mass aligns closely with direct measurements from laboratory-reared larvae collected in the upper Sutlej River drainage. Newly emerged prolarvae retain a prominent yolk sac for approximately five to seven days, during which they remain largely sedentary among gravel interstices before transitioning to active planktonic feeding.

Breeding adults of Snowtrout attain an ultimate wet weight of 2350 grams [Wwi = 2350 grams], a body mass that enables them to dominate spawning riffles and produce large clutches during the brief summer reproductive window. This asymptotic mass is typically reached after several years of steady growth in the cold, food-limited environments characteristic of their native range. Gravid females in this mass class have been documented carrying substantial ovarian loads, with fecundity estimates reaching several thousand oocytes per spawning event. The maximum record of 2350 grams [Wwi = 2350 grams] represents an upper bound observed in long-term mark-recapture studies, though most individuals in exploited populations rarely exceed 2000 grams. The energetic cost of maintaining such a large body in fast-flowing, oxygen-saturated waters is considerable, but the payoff in terms of competitive ability on spawning grounds and total lifetime reproductive output appears to justify this investment under pristine conditions.

Longevity records derived from otolith annuli counts of individuals collected in a relatively undisturbed section of the Yarlung Tsangpo drainage at 9 °C [T = 9 °C] indicate a maximum life span of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years]. This extended lifespan is among the greatest reported for any cyprinid of comparable body size and is intimately linked to the persistently low water temperatures that characterise its alpine habitat. The cold thermal regime dramatically depresses metabolic rates, slows the accumulation of cellular damage, and imposes a slow pace of life that translates directly into delayed senescence. In warmer tributaries where summer maxima approach 15 to 18 °C, anecdotal evidence suggests that maximum age is substantially reduced, though no formal comparative study has yet been conducted across thermal gradients. The interplay between temperature and lifespan in this species provides a compelling natural laboratory for examining the thermal dependence of ageing in freshwater fishes.

The protracted lifespan of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] has profound implications for the species' population dynamics and vulnerability to exploitation at a temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. Populations experiencing even moderate fishing pressure may lose their oldest, most fecund individuals before these fish have contributed more than a few spawning seasons, potentially destabilising the age structure and reducing recruitment over time. Comparative data from other long-lived Schizothorax species indicate that the combination of high ultimate body mass, here 2350 grams [Wwi = 2350 grams], and slow maturation places a premium on adult survival and repeated reproductive events. At 9 °C, the metabolic cost of a single spawning season is spread across a lengthy period of gonadal recrudescence, allowing females to allocate energy toward both somatic maintenance and egg production without catastrophic lipid depletion. Conservation strategies for this species must therefore account for the low intrinsic replacement rate dictated by its cold-water life history.
